An AI agent reproduces chaos faster than any human. That's exactly why we're betting our back office on it.

Give an agent a company without written rules, and it invents ten intake procedures by lunchtime, none matching what accounting expects. Give it the rules, and you get an employee who follows them to the letter, every time, with no bad days. There is no better keeper of the owner's rules than an AI agent. The whole job is to have the rules.

We service fuel station networks and oil depots: a handful of people, hundreds of client sites, the usual grind of requests, work orders, acts, invoices, timesheets.

The normal path is to hire a dispatcher, a bookkeeper, an HR clerk, a document controller. We built a harness of agents instead — not a team: agents don't choose where to go, they pull where the owner steers. It's ready for live operation at pilot sites.

The rule is blunt: not a single manual entry by a human into any document or application. The engineer turns wrenches; agents do everything about documents and data; the owner approves results from a control desk.

Three layers. Owner on top. Agents in the middle: dispatcher, bookkeeper, HR, treasurer, contract manager. Field people at the bottom. Agents replace the layer between them — where a request is retyped from an email into a system, an act into an invoice, a timesheet cross-checked against work orders. In a normal company that layer eats three to five salaries and half the owner's week.

So before the first line of code we wrote some twenty internal rules: who owns what, which documents exist, how they move, who approves, what is personal data. First question to any owner who wants "to implement AI": do you have a document register and a responsibility matrix? If not, that's where the project starts and where the money goes.

An agent is an employee. Every HR term got a technical meaning.
• Hiring: a passport — purpose, access, permitted operations, owner — in a register.
• Probation: works in the shadow while a human does the same job. Pass mark: 70–85% of documents accepted without edits.
• Work mode: approve (agent prepares, human signs), notify (agent acts, human can revert), auto (agent acts, human sees the log). The table "operation — mode — approver" is the master document.
• Appraisal: continuous. Three weeks above threshold — next mode. Same rules downward.
• Dismissal: by act, with log handover and access revoked.

Legal line: an agent is a tool with an account, no legal personality; the company is liable. Anything it produces is a draft until a human signs. Money, people, client obligations stay in approve mode.

Data: personal data never leaves the country and runs on local models. External models get anonymised documents only, from a list the owner signs. No document names a model vendor: the method stays, the tool is replaceable.

Which operation in your company would you not trust to notify mode?

A new law in Italy draws a clear line: AI can help with staff decisions, but a person has to make them.

Italy's AI decree, number 179 of 2026, took effect on 23 October. Under article 41, final decisions on hiring, contract changes, dismissal, discipline and performance reviews cannot be based solely on automated processing. Decisions made in breach are void. The rule applies to employers of any size, and staff consent does not override it.

For businesses outside Italy, the rule is not binding. We still think it is the standard worth working to, because it describes what good use of AI looks like. The machine does the preparation. The owner, who knows the people, does the deciding.

What we suggest this week:
1. Write down where AI already feeds into decisions about your team, including scheduling tools and CV screening.
2. Make one named person responsible for the final decision in each case.
3. Record, briefly, what the AI produced and what the person decided. It takes a minute and protects everyone.

Before pasting anything about an employee into an AI tool, remove their name and personal details, and check the tool's privacy settings.

Founders: your AI just approved, rejected or flagged a real person. Is that legal under GDPR? 🤖

Article 22 GDPR gives people the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that has legal or similarly significant effects on them. Profiling itself is allowed with a lawful basis, but the stakes rise fast once a model decides who gets a loan, a job or an account.

Why it matters for startups:
🔹 AI features in hiring, lending, insurance and fraud tools often fall squarely in scope
🔹 A rubber-stamp human review is not meaningful human involvement
🔹 Training data is personal data processing too, with its own lawful basis questions

What a GDPR-ready AI feature needs:
✅ A lawful basis for both training and use (Art. 6)
✅ For Art. 22 decisions: contract necessity, legal authorisation or explicit consent (Art. 22(2))
✅ Safeguards: human intervention, a chance to give views and contest (Art. 22(3))
✅ Meaningful information about the logic involved (Art. 13(2)(f), 15(1)(h))
✅ A DPIA where risk is high (Art. 35), plus data minimisation and retention limits

Smart models still need lawful decisions.

𝟓 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐈'𝐝 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐛𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞.

When a team is overwhelmed, hiring more people often feels like the most obvious solution.
But before adding headcount, I'd ask one question:

𝐀𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐭 𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞, 𝐨𝐫 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐞 𝐚𝐬𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐝𝐨 𝐭𝐨𝐨 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐞?

In many businesses, a significant amount of operational capacity is tied up in repetitive tasks, manual handoffs, and information processing. Adding more people may help in the short term, but it doesn't necessarily solve the underlying problem.
Here are five processes I'd look at first.

𝟏. 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐨𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠
A finance team receives hundreds of invoices in different formats. Employees manually extract data, enter it into the ERP, and check for errors.
AI can extract key fields, validate information, and flag discrepancies for human review.

𝟐. 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧
Every week, managers collect spreadsheets from different departments, reconcile inconsistent figures, and prepare reports.
Automate data collection and consolidation, then use AI to summarize trends and highlight anomalies.

𝟑. 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐧𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠
A new customer signs a contract, but onboarding stalls because documents are missing, approvals are pending, or nobody follows up.
Workflow automation can assign tasks, send reminders, track progress, and escalate delays automatically.

𝟒. 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭
Support teams repeatedly answer questions about order status, account procedures, or common issues.
AI agents can retrieve approved information, answer routine questions, and route complex cases to the right person.

𝟓. 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐝𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧
After every client meeting, salespeople need to update CRM, summarize discussions, log next steps, and send follow-up emails.

AI can draft meeting summaries, update relevant records, and prepare follow-ups for review, leaving salespeople more time to engage prospects.

The important part: 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬 𝐀𝐈. Some need workflow automation. Others need better system integration or process redesign.

Before hiring more people, identify where your existing team is spending time on repetitive work, and calculate whether automating it makes business sense.

That's a much better starting point than adding headcount by default.

Your AI Assistant Doesn't Know Your Business. RAG Fixes That.

Ask a general AI tool about your refund policy, your pricing tiers or last quarter's supplier contract, and you'll get one of two things: a polite guess or a confident wrong answer. Neither helps when a customer is waiting.

The reason is simple. These models learned from the public internet. They've never seen your documents.

That's the gap RAG closes. It stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and the idea is easy to explain. Before the AI answers, it first looks up the relevant pieces of your own material, such as product manuals, FAQs, policies and past tickets, and writes its answer from what it found. Think of an open-book exam instead of a memory test.

Why this matters for a business:

- Answers match your real policies. The AI quotes your documents, not the internet's average opinion.
- Updates are quick. Change a price list today and the answers change today. No retraining, no waiting.
- Fewer made-up answers. When the AI has to work from your sources, it's far less likely to invent things.
- Your team gets time back. The repetitive questions about hours, delivery, returns and "where's my order" stop landing on your staff.
- It scales without hiring. Ten customers or ten thousand, the answer quality stays the same.

Most of your customers are already on Telegram, Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp. That's where they ask questions, usually at odd hours. A RAG assistant connected to those channels can answer from your own knowledge base around the clock, and pass the tricky cases to a human.

I help businesses set this up: a Telegram bot or social media assistant that knows your products, your policies and your tone, and handles the routine conversations so you can focus on the work that grows the business.

In Westworld, Dr. Robert Ford didn’t write faster algorithms to make hosts conscious. He gave them three architectural pillars:

"You are an expert PM agent. Write clear tickets."
"You are a DevOps agent. Monitor clusters."
No history. Zero friction. Memory wiped every session. Then we wonder why multi-agent systems feel plastic, sycophantic, and incapable of hard trade-offs.
A bot without a backstory has no point of view.
A bot without a cornerstone has no conviction.
---
Hiring the Epics: Cognitive Archetype Matrix
Every civilization preserved archetypes of extreme decision-making. Today, we can hire them as operating lenses in agent loops:
• 🇮🇳 Chanakya (Kautilya):
Cornerstone: Royal humiliation & foreign invasion threat.
Lens: Audits incentives over words; demands structural defensibility.
Deploy: Partner API contracts, data-moat validation, vendor bots.
• 🏛️ Marcus Aurelius:
Cornerstone: Imperial duty & plague burden.
Lens: Radical friction-dampener; halts velocity when principles breach.
Deploy: Governance plane, safety circuit breakers, legal CI gates.
• 🇨🇳 Sun Tzu:
Cornerstone: Warring States resource scarcity.
Lens: Ruthless economy of force; win without fighting.
Deploy: Token & GPU cost optimizer, cache routing, tree pruning.
• 🇮🇹 Machiavelli:
Cornerstone: Collapse of Florence from idealism.
Lens: Stark realism; audits human self-interest and politics.
Deploy: Enterprise change management, rollout triage, adoption bots.
• 🛠️ The SRE Skeptic:
Cornerstone: 3 AM silent schema crash.
Lens: Paranoid auditor; trusts zero unverified diffs.
Deploy: Pull request review nodes (Paperclip, Firstmate, GitHub Actions).
---
Teams of Bots: The Power of Productive Tension
Amateur multi-agent systems optimize for harmony: five bots politely validating each other in an echo chamber.
In production, harmony is catastrophe. Real intelligence emerges from productive tension:
- Paranoid Auditor: Remembers silent schema breaks; rejects unverified diffs.
- Velocity Builder: Biased to action; obsessed with shipping real code.
- Sovereign Strategist (Chanakya): Audits unit economics and moats.
When these three argue inside your harness, they aren’t wasting tokens. They are stress-testing reality before software touches customers.
---
Stop treating agent prompts like static YAML configs.
1. Define its Cornerstone (the non-negotiable trade-off).
2. Define its Imperfections (what it deliberately ignores).
3. Give it Reveries (living episodic memory across loops).
We are directing cognitive ensembles.
If you could encode ONE historical or fictional mind into your CI/CD pipeline tomorrow, who are you hiring?

The most expensive line in your AI budget is the judgement you didn't hire.

Most boards are being shown AI-enabled supply chain savings this year. Very few of those numbers survive a second question.

A global coffee chain now counts inventory with cameras. The app mislabels the milk. Four CEOs in five years have blamed empty shelves for lost sales. The software worked — the network beneath it could not be modelled cleanly.

A footwear brand's planning system ordered too much of the slow sellers and too little of the bestsellers: $100 million in lost sales, 20% off the share price in a day. The algorithm wasn't the failure. No one ever met to review the forecast.

And better data doesn't rescue you. A study of 4,523 grocery products found sharper forecasts cut inventory while making ordering up to 31% more erratic. The model had no view of which trade-off the business wanted.

Same gap every time. Not modelling. Judgement.

Closing it is not a hiring-volume problem. It is a rare-profile problem. Most operators spend their careers inside the systems they inherited. Most AI people have never owned a service level, a detention charge or a cold-chain excursion. The few who can read the P&L and interrogate the model at the same time will be the ones global supply chains are built around this decade. Where an organisation has one, the advantage compounds. Where it doesn't, it keeps buying models and calling it transformation.

As a global supply chain director owning the whole chain, not a function: ports, CFS, yards, FTWZ, warehousing, 3PL/4PL, contract logistics, cold chain, rail, express, freight forwarding. One AI layer above those core systems so they plan from the same numbers. Above it, a quantum layer held honestly — hybrid today, classical still winning; the formulation is the moat, not the hardware.

That is where I work: domain on one side, AI on the other, and the number in between with my name on it. It is the least comfortable place to stand in this industry, and the most useful.

The scarce hire isn't the person who can buy the model. It's the one who can overrule it.

If you're approving AI supply chain savings nobody in the room can stress-test, that exposure is already on your P&L. It just hasn't been booked yet.

I'd rather argue about this than post about it. 

DMs open.
